---
title: "Convex Sets"
---

These exercises are adapted from @cvxbook.

::: {#exr-finite-convex-combinations name="Finite convex combinations" .exercise}
Let $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex set, with $x_1, \ldots, x_k \in C$, and let $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_k \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$
\theta_i \geq 0,
\qquad
\theta_1 + \cdots + \theta_k = 1.
$$

Show that

$$
\theta_1x_1 + \cdots + \theta_kx_k \in C.
$$

The definition of convexity gives this result for $k=2$; prove it for arbitrary $k$.

*Hint.* Use induction on $k$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

We prove the result by induction on the number of points.

The case $k=1$ is immediate: the coefficient condition forces $\theta_1=1$, so $\theta_1x_1=x_1\in C$.

For the first nontrivial case, let $k=2$. If $x_1,x_2\in C$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, then the definition of convexity gives

$$
(1-\theta)x_1+\theta x_2\in C.
$$

Thus every convex combination of two points in $C$ belongs to $C$.

Now suppose every convex combination of $\ell$ points in $C$ belongs to $C$. In other words, whenever

$$
x_i\in C,
\qquad
\theta_i\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\theta_i=1,
$$

we have

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\theta_i x_i\in C.
$$

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell+1}\in C$, and let $\phi_i\geq0$ satisfy

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i=1.
$$

If $\phi_{\ell+1}=1$, then $\phi_1=\cdots=\phi_\ell=0$, so

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i=x_{\ell+1}\in C.
$$

Now suppose $\phi_{\ell+1}<1$, and define

$$
z=\frac{1}{1-\phi_{\ell+1}}
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i x_i.
$$

Since

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i=1-\phi_{\ell+1},
$$

the coefficients in the definition of $z$ are nonnegative and sum to one. The induction hypothesis therefore implies that $z\in C$.

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i
&=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i x_i+\phi_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1} \\
&=(1-\phi_{\ell+1})z+\phi_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $z,x_{\ell+1}\in C$ and $\phi_{\ell+1}\in[0,1]$, convexity of $C$ gives

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i\in C.
$$

Therefore, by induction, every finite convex combination of points in $C$ belongs to $C$.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-parallel-hyperplanes-distance name="Distance between parallel hyperplanes" .exercise}
For $a\neq0$, what is the distance between the parallel hyperplanes

$$
H_1=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid a^Tx=b_1\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
H_2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid a^Tx=b_2\}?
$$

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

For every $x_1\in H_1$ and $x_2\in H_2$,

$$
a^T(x_1-x_2)=b_1-b_2.
$$

The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality therefore gives

$$
|b_1-b_2|
=|a^T(x_1-x_2)|
\leq\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert.
$$

Thus every pair of points, one from each hyperplane, satisfies

$$
\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert
\geq
\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}.
$$

This lower bound is attained. Choose any $x_2\in H_2$ and define

$$
x_1=x_2+\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a.
$$

Then

$$
a^Tx_1
=a^Tx_2+\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a^Ta
=b_2+(b_1-b_2)
=b_1,
$$

so $x_1\in H_1$, and

$$
\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert
=\left\lVert\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a\right\rVert
=\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}.
$$

Hence the distance between the hyperplanes is

$$
\boxed{\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}}.
$$
:::
:::

::: {#exr-voronoi-halfspace name="Voronoi description of a halfspace" .exercise}
Let $a$ and $b$ be distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Show that the set of all points that are closer in Euclidean norm to $a$ than to $b$,

$$
\{x\mid \lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2\},
$$

is a halfspace. Describe it explicitly as an inequality of the form $c^Tx\leq d$. Draw a picture.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Since both sides are nonnegative,

$$
\lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2
\iff
\lVert x-a\rVert_2^2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2^2.
$$

Expanding the squared norms gives

$$
\lVert x-a\rVert_2^2=x^Tx-2a^Tx+a^Ta,
\qquad
\lVert x-b\rVert_2^2=x^Tx-2b^Tx+b^Tb.
$$

The quadratic terms cancel, leaving

$$
2(b-a)^Tx\leq b^Tb-a^Ta.
$$

Thus

$$
\{x\mid\lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2\}
=
\{x\mid c^Tx\leq d\},
$$

where

$$
c=b-a,
\qquad
d=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\lVert b\rVert_2^2-\lVert a\rVert_2^2\bigr).
$$

Since $a\neq b$, we have $c\neq0$, so this is a halfspace. Geometrically, its boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment $[a,b]$, and the halfspace contains $a$.
:::
:::
